alt: Two columns. Common law rules are defined with cases: murder (Vickers), unlawful act and gross negligence manslaughter (Church, Adomako), assault and battery, and the general defences. Statutory rules are quoted first: loss of control, diminished responsibility, s47, s20, s18, theft, robbery and attempt. Self-defence combines both. Judges interpret statutes (Ireland and Burstow; Gomez) but no longer create offences (Knuller), and there is no criminal code.
caption: Define common law offences with cases; quote statutory wording, then the cases.

alt: The prosecution bears the legal burden to prove every element beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington). For self-defence, duress, automatism, intoxication and loss of control the defendant only raises evidence and the prosecution must disprove the defence beyond reasonable doubt. For insanity and diminished responsibility the defendant bears a reverse burden on the balance of probabilities.
caption: Most defences only need raising; insanity and diminished responsibility must be proved.

alt: The judge decides questions of law: what an offence means, whether a defence goes to the jury and how to direct the jury. The jury decides facts by applying those directions. Examples: in attempt the judge asks whether there is evidence an act could be more than merely preparatory and the jury decides if it was; in theft the jury applies the Ivey test for dishonesty; in murder the jury may find intention under Woollin but is not obliged to.
caption: The judge says what the law requires; the jury decides whether the facts meet it.

alt: Offences sorted by DPP v Majewski. Specific intent, where only intention will do: murder, s18, theft, robbery and attempt. Basic intent, where recklessness is enough: manslaughter, s20, s47, assault and battery. The split matters most for intoxication and helps in choosing alternative charges.
caption: Specific intent needs intention; basic intent can be satisfied by recklessness.

alt: Offences ranked by maximum sentence: murder (mandatory life); s18 and robbery (life); theft (seven years); s47 and s20 (five years); assault and battery (six months, summary). If the mens rea for a higher offence fails, move down the ladder, for example s18 to s20. Attempt carries the same maximum as the full offence.
caption: Start at the top of the ladder and move down when an element fails.

after: ## Applying the rules: a method for problem questions
alt: Seven steps: identify the most serious offence and victim; state the rule and its source; give authority for disputed elements; apply to the facts; consider alternatives down the ladder; consider defences and the burden; conclude on likely liability.
caption: Source, element, authority, application, conclusion: the skeleton of every answer.

alt: Ed’s case worked down the ladder. s18 fails: the fracture is really serious harm (DPP v Smith) but Ed did not intend GBH. s20 is satisfied: GBH was inflicted (Burstow) and Ed foresaw some harm (Mowatt). No defences apply, so Ed is likely guilty under s20, a basic intent offence with a five-year maximum.
caption: Start at the top, explain why it fails, and move down.
